questions.q: A student places five things on one timeline: bhakti saints choosing devotion (7th to 17th centuries), Marathi writing (from the 12th century), Yadava rule at Devagiri (13th century), the Khilji conquest of Devagiri (early 14th century) and Chhatrapati Shivaji's birth (1630). Which two items were still going on after the Khilji conquest and before 1630?
questions.a: Marathi writing and the bhakti tradition
o: Marathi writing and the bhakti tradition
Yadava rule at Devagiri and Marathi writing
The Khilji conquest and the bhakti tradition
Yadava rule at Devagiri and the bhakti tradition

questions.q: Write a quiz question about Maharashtra before Chhatrapati Shivaji whose only correct answer is 'the Khilji Sultanate'. Then give two details from the chapter that a student would need to answer it.
questions.a: Sample question: 'Which power from Delhi overcame the dynasty that ruled most of Maharashtra from Devagiri?' Details: in the 13th century the Yadava dynasty ruled most of Maharashtra with Devagiri (present-day Daulatabad) as its capital; in the early 14th century the Yadavas were overcome by the Khilji Sultanate from Delhi.
s: A question with the Khilji Sultanate as its only answer
Detail 1: Yadava rule from Devagiri in the 13th century
Detail 2: the Khilji conquest from Delhi in the early 14th century

questions.q:
A library in Pune lists its old Marathi manuscripts by century (illustrative figures, not from the book): 12th century 3, 13th century 9, 14th century 14, 15th century 11, 16th century 18, 17th century 27. Every century from the 12th to the 17th has at least some works.
(a) Which term defined in the chapter describes what an unbroken run like this, in one language, shows?
(b) The 14th-century count is higher than the 13th, even though Devagiri fell to rulers from Delhi in that century. Which statement in the chapter explains why this is not surprising?
(c) Chhatrapati Shivaji was born in 1630. What percentage of the listed manuscripts come from his birth century and the century before it? Give one decimal place.
(d) A visitor says the list proves that Chhatrapati Shivaji's kingdom caused the 17th-century rise. Judge this claim using the chapter's dates.
questions.a: (a) Literary history: the historical development of writings in prose or poetry in a particular language; the list shows Marathi's continuous literary history. (b) The chapter says that amidst political changes, such as the Khilji Sultanate overcoming the Yadavas, the cultural traditions continued, particularly bhakti, so writing did not stop. (c) Total = 3 + 9 + 14 + 11 + 18 + 27 = 82; his birth century (17th, 27) and the 16th (18) = 45; 45 / 82 x 100 = 54.9%. (d) The claim is not proved. A count by century cannot show a cause, and the 17th century runs from 1601 to 1700, while Chhatrapati Shivaji was born in 1630, began his rule in 1646 and was crowned in 1674, so many 17th-century works may be older than his kingdom.
s: Part (a): literary history (continuous development of writing in one language)
Part (b): cultural traditions continued amidst political changes
Part (c): 45 of 82, about 54.9%
Part (d): not proved; a count shows no cause, and many 17th-century works may predate his kingdom

questions.q: A guide at Daulatabad tells a school group: 'The Khilji Sultanate from Delhi overcame the Yadava capital here in 1250.' Using the chapter's dating, what is wrong with her statement?
questions.a: Yadavas ruled from Devagiri in the 13th century; the Khiljis came in the early 14th
o: Yadavas ruled from Devagiri in the 13th century; the Khiljis came in the early 14th
The Khiljis ruled Maharashtra from Devagiri, so they could not have come from Delhi
Devagiri was never a Yadava capital; the Yadavas ruled from Delhi until 1250
The Yadavas were overcome by the Bijapur Sultanate, not by the Khiljis at all

questions.q: The chapter defines literary history as the historical development of writings in prose or poetry in a particular language. Four students choose projects. Whose project is a study of Marathi literary history?
questions.a: Meera traces how Marathi poems and prose changed from the 12th century onwards
o: Meera traces how Marathi poems and prose changed from the 12th century onwards
Kabir lists the dynasties that ruled Devagiri between the 13th and 14th centuries
Ananya maps the districts of the Deccan plateau where Marathi is spoken today
Rohan counts the neglected forts around Pune that were captured and repaired

questions.q: Say whether this is True or False and give the reason: 'When the Khilji Sultanate from Delhi overcame the Yadava dynasty, the bhakti tradition of Maharashtra came to an end.'
questions.a: False. The chapter says that amidst such political changes the cultural traditions continued, particularly bhakti; the bhakti path ran from the 7th to the 17th centuries, and saints in Maharashtra went on translating texts such as the Bhagavad Gita into Marathi.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: cultural traditions, especially bhakti, continued through the change of rulers (bhakti spans the 7th to 17th centuries)

questions.q: Riya's notebook reads: 'Before Chhatrapati Shivaji, the Marathas had nothing in common; they became one people only when he united them.' Is this supported by the chapter?
questions.a: No. Before Chhatrapati Shivaji the Marathas already shared a land (the Deccan plateau, present-day Maharashtra) and a language (Marathi, with a continuous literary history since the 12th century), and the bhakti saints had given society a solid cultural foundation. What they lacked was political unity: early attempts by some chiefs at sovereignty failed until Chhatrapati Shivaji brought them together. So he united them politically, but they did not start with nothing in common.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Evidence of what they shared before him: land, Marathi language and literary history, bhakti culture
What he actually added: political unity after earlier chiefs' attempts failed

questions.q: The chapter says the bhakti path was followed from the 7th to the 17th century. Chhatrapati Shivaji was born in 1630, so his boyhood fell in the ___ century, still within that span.
questions.a: 17th

questions.q: Give two reasons from the chapter why the message of the bhakti saints of Maharashtra could reach ordinary farmers and workers, which a message written only in a scholars' language could not.
questions.a: Any two of: saints composed songs and poetry in the languages of the masses, so ordinary people could understand them; texts such as the Upanishads and the Bhagavad Gita were translated into Marathi, making their philosophy accessible; the songs and poetry could therefore travel far and wide.
s: First reason: songs and poetry in the languages of the masses
Second reason: translations of texts into Marathi, so the message travelled far and wide

questions.q:
Place these six items in order of when they began and then use the order to answer the question that follows: Marathi's literary history (12th century), the Yadava rule from Devagiri (13th century), the Khilji conquest of Devagiri (early 14th century), the bhakti tradition (from the 7th century), Maratha chiefs' attempts at sovereignty (by the 17th century), and Chhatrapati Shivaji's birth (1630).
(a) Give the order from earliest to latest start.
(b) Which two items ran through every political change in the list, and which two came after them?
(c) What does this order show about whether the culture or the dynasties were steadier in Maharashtra?
questions.a: (a) Bhakti tradition (7th century); Marathi literary history (12th century); Yadava rule from Devagiri (13th century); Khilji conquest (early 14th century); chiefs' early attempts at sovereignty (by the 17th century); Shivaji's birth (1630). (b) The bhakti tradition and Marathi writing ran through the Yadava and Khilji changes; the chiefs' attempts and Shivaji's birth came after. (c) The dynasties changed from Yadava to Khilji within about a century, while the culture kept going: the chapter says amidst political changes the cultural traditions continued, particularly bhakti, and Marathi's literary history is continuous. So culture was the steadier thread, and sovereignty came last, after the culture had been built.
s: Bhakti and Marathi writing placed first
Yadava rule and the Khilji conquest placed next
Chiefs' attempts and Shivaji's birth placed last
The two items that ran through every political change identified
Conclusion: culture was steadier than dynasties, and political power came last

questions.q:

Reason (R): Marathi has had a rich and continuous literary history since the 12th century.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: 'The Marathas had a shared identity long before they had a kingdom.' Justify this statement with evidence about their land, language and culture, and explain what was still missing until the 17th century.
questions.a: Land: the Marathas are native to the Deccan plateau, more specifically present-day Maharashtra. Language: they are identified with Marathi, which has had a rich and continuous literary history since the 12th century. Culture: between the 7th and 17th centuries bhakti saints from diverse sections of society sang in the languages of the masses; in Maharashtra saints such as Dnyaneshwar, Namdev, Tukaram and Ramdas helped translate the Upanishads and the Bhagavad Gita into Marathi, and some worked on social organisation and political awareness. This continued even when rulers changed from the Yadavas to the Khiljis. Missing: political unity and sovereignty. Early attempts by some Maratha chiefs failed until Chhatrapati Shivaji rose to power and brought the Marathas together.
s: Land: native to the Deccan plateau, present-day Maharashtra
Language: Marathi with a continuous literary history since the 12th century
Culture: bhakti saints, songs in the people's language, translations into Marathi
Continuity through the change from Yadava to Khilji rule
What was missing: political unity, until Chhatrapati Shivaji succeeded where earlier chiefs failed

questions.q:
(a) The chapter says bhakti means devotion to the divine or a particular deity, and that saints preferred it to merely external ritualism. Scene X: a trader pays for a long ceremony and follows every step exactly, certain that correct steps are what matter. Scene Y: a weaver sings a Marathi song of devotion to her deity while she works. Which scene shows the bhakti path the saints preferred?
(b) Give the reason the chapter offers for saints choosing that path, and say what Scene X shows the saints preferred it to.
questions.a: (a) Scene Y: devotion expressed in the people's own language. (b) The chapter says saints chose bhakti for spiritual upliftment; Scene X shows the merely external ritualism that they preferred bhakti to.
s: Part (a): Scene Y, devotion rather than ritual
Part (b): chosen for spiritual upliftment; Scene X is the external ritualism they moved away from

questions.q: The chapter says some saints of Maharashtra were 'similar to the Sikh gurus'. State the point of similarity and explain why that point matters in a chapter about a political power.
questions.a: The similarity is that some saints focused on social organisation and political awareness, not only on devotion. It matters because this helped society acquire a solid cultural foundation, which later helped the Marathas organise themselves into a political power.
s: Point of similarity: focus on social organisation and political awareness
Why it matters: it prepared the ground for the Marathas to organise politically later

questions.q:
(a) A Marathi-speaking farmer in the 16th century cannot read Sanskrit. Using the chapter, say what the Maharashtra saints' translations made possible for him.
(b) Explain how the chapter links this kind of work to the later rise of the Marathas as a political power.
questions.a: (a) The saints helped translate texts such as the Upanishads and the Bhagavad Gita into Marathi, so their philosophy became accessible to him in his own language. (b) Work like this gave society a solid cultural foundation, which the chapter says later helped the Marathas organise themselves into a political power.
s: Part (a): translations of the Upanishads and Bhagavad Gita into Marathi made their philosophy accessible to him
Part (b): this built a solid cultural foundation that later helped the Marathas organise politically

questions.q:
Two students answer 'What prepared the Marathas for political power?' Asha: 'Only the bhakti saints; the Marathas organised themselves into a political power through bhakti alone.' Bilal: 'Bhakti gave a cultural foundation, but the chapter says early attempts by some chiefs failed until a leader brought the Marathas together.'
(a) What does the chapter say bhakti gave society, and what did it later help the Marathas do?
(b) What does the chapter say about the Maratha chiefs' early attempts to establish sovereignty?
(c) Whose answer is better supported by the chapter, and why?
(d) Predict what the chapter implies about the Marathas' political fate if the bhakti foundation had existed but no leader like Chhatrapati Shivaji had risen.
questions.a: (a) A solid cultural foundation, which later helped the Marathas organise themselves into a political power. (b) By the 17th century some chiefs made early attempts at establishing sovereignty, but they proved unsuccessful. (c) Bilal's. The chapter says bhakti 'later helped' the Marathas, a help and not the sole cause, and it says the attempts failed until Chhatrapati Shivaji rose to power and brought the Marathas together; Asha's 'only' and 'alone' go beyond the chapter. (d) The foundation alone would not have been enough: the chapter shows the chiefs' attempts at sovereignty failing without such a leader, so the Marathas would probably have remained without a sovereign kingdom.
s: Part (a): a solid cultural foundation that later helped political organisation
Part (b): early attempts by some chiefs were unsuccessful
Part (c): Bilal's; bhakti helped but did not alone cause the rise, and the leader's role is stated
Part (d): foundation without a leader would not have been enough, as the failed attempts show

questions.q: A tourist poster says: 'Marathi literature was born at the court of Chhatrapati Shivaji.' Using only dates and facts from the chapter, show that this cannot be true.
questions.a: Chhatrapati Shivaji was born in 1630, in the 17th century, and his rule began in 1646. The chapter says Marathi has had a rich and continuous literary history since the 12th century, about five centuries before his birth. A tradition that was already continuous for centuries before he was born cannot have been born at his court, so the poster's claim is impossible.
s: Shivaji's dates: born 1630, rule from 1646 (17th century)
Marathi literary history continuous from the 12th century
Conclusion: a tradition centuries older than him cannot have begun at his court

questions.a: (a) Shahji served the Deccan sultanates, so he was often away from his family. (b) Jijabai and some trusted officials brought him up in the jagir at Pune, and he received values and a good education.

questions.q:
Rahul reads that in 1646 Chhatrapati Shivaji, then 16, was working in and around Pune, and that the chapter's timeline puts the founding of the Maratha navy in 1657. He is puzzled: 'Pune is inland. How can a navy come out of it?'
(a) Between his early campaigns and the navy, what had happened to the kingdom's extent, according to the chapter?
(b) What did the chapter say he felt the need for once this had happened, and why?
(c) What did the Bijapur Sultanate and the Mughal Empire have at sea, according to the chapter?
(d) Explain why there is no real contradiction in Rahul's puzzle.
questions.a: (a) The kingdom expanded to India's west coast. (b) He felt the need to establish a navy, to secure access to the resources of the coastal regions. (c) Bijapur maintained merchant ships but had no full-time naval force that could protect the coast, and the Mughal Empire's use of a navy was very limited. (d) The navy was not built from Pune; it came only after the kingdom grew from the Pune region to the west coast, which took the years between 1646 and 1657, and the chapter says the coast was where the need arose.
s: Part (a): the kingdom expanded to the west coast
Part (b): a navy, to secure coastal resources
Part (c): Bijapur merchant ships only; Mughal use very limited
Part (d): the navy followed the expansion to the coast, so Pune's being inland is no contradiction

questions.q: The chapter gives a different aim for each of two steps Chhatrapati Shivaji took: founding a navy, and using guerrilla warfare. Match each step to the aim the chapter gives for it.
questions.a: The navy was founded to secure access to the resources of the coastal regions once the kingdom reached the west coast. Guerrilla warfare was used to protect his people from powerful enemies, defeating bigger armies with small, fast groups.
s: Navy: to secure access to the resources of the coastal regions
Guerrilla warfare: to protect his people from powerful enemies with bigger armies

questions.q: A quiz card says: 'Chhatrapati Shivaji's first step to power was building a navy.' Using the chapter's facts and dates, show that this cannot be true.
questions.a: His rule began in 1646, when at 16 he first consolidated his hold over the Pune region by capturing neglected and unoccupied forts and strengthening their defences. The navy was founded only in 1657, eleven years later, and only after his kingdom had expanded to India's west coast and he needed to secure the coastal resources. A navy could not come first, because the kingdom did not yet reach the coast when his campaigns began.
s: First step: in 1646, capturing and strengthening neglected forts around Pune
Navy founded in 1657, eleven years later
The navy needed the kingdom to reach the west coast first, so it could not be the first step

questions.q: A classmate's profile of the young Chhatrapati Shivaji reads: 'He grew up in comfort and peace, far from the troubles of the Deccan.' Test it against the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. The care is right: he grew up under the watchful eyes of Jijabai and some trusted officials and received values and a good education. The peace is wrong: the Pune region was deeply affected by constant infighting between the Deccan sultans, which caused much hardship for the common people, so he was not far from the Deccan's troubles.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: careful upbringing by Jijabai and officials, with values and education
Wrong part: Pune suffered from the sultans' infighting and hardship

questions.q: Explain why, according to the chapter, the Maratha navy was 'a truly revolutionary step' on the west coast. Use what it says about the Bijapur Sultanate and the Mughal Empire.
questions.a: The Bijapur Sultanate, ruled by the Adil Shahi dynasty, maintained merchant ships but did not possess a full-time naval force that could protect the coast. The Mughal Empire's use of a navy was very limited. So when Chhatrapati Shivaji created a navy to secure the resources of the coast, he did something neither neighbour had done, which made it revolutionary.
s: Bijapur had merchant ships but no full-time naval force to protect the coast
The Mughal use of a navy was very limited
So a navy built for the coast was a new step neither power had taken

questions.q:
A school history club runs a war-game (invented for this question). Team Sahyadri has 1,800 foot soldiers who know every path of a thickly forested hill valley, and a few old, unguarded hill forts stand in the valley. Team Plains has 13,500 soldiers with heavy cannon, used to fighting in open fields.
(a) How many times larger is Team Plains than Team Sahyadri?
(b) Name the tactic from this chapter that Team Sahyadri should use, and give two of its features that the valley offers them.
(c) Team Sahyadri's captain wants to take and repair the old hill forts first. Using the chapter, give one reason forts help a side that fights in this way.
(d) Team Plains offers two terms: fight in the valley at dawn, or on an open plain at noon, announced a day earlier. Decide which Team Sahyadri should accept and say what the other choice would cost it.
questions.a: (a) 13,500 / 1,800 = 7.5 times. (b) Guerrilla warfare: small groups used in a focused way, with speed, surprise and knowledge of the terrain; the valley gives knowledge of the terrain and forest cover that makes surprise possible. (c) The chapter says forts were essential to strategically control important routes and to shelter the army when engaging in guerrilla warfare. (d) The valley at dawn. Guerrilla warfare depends on surprise and knowledge of the terrain; on an open plain, announced a day before, neither is available and numbers and cannon decide, which favours the 7.5-times larger army.
s: Part (a): 7.5 times
Part (b): guerrilla warfare, with terrain knowledge and surprise (or speed) offered by the valley
Part (c): forts shelter the army and control routes
Part (d): the valley, since the plain removes surprise and terrain knowledge and leaves numbers to decide

questions.q:
(a) Which two features of the meeting place at Pratapgad, as the chapter describes it, helped the hidden Marathas?
(b) The wagh nakh is described as a tiger's-claw-shaped weapon used in close combat. Say why a one-on-one meeting suited that weapon.

questions.q: State True or False, and correct it if False: 'Chhatrapati Shivaji's Swarajya meant only control of territory through captured forts.'

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Once his kingdom expanded to India's west coast, Chhatrapati Shivaji felt the need to establish a navy.
Reason (R): He wanted to secure access to the resources of the coastal regions.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.q:
(a) Name the first military step the chapter says Chhatrapati Shivaji took when he was 16.
(b) Use your answer to explain how its purpose differed from the purpose of the navy he founded later.
questions.a: (a) He consolidated his hold over the Pune region by capturing neglected and unoccupied forts and strengthening their defences. (b) The forts secured his base around Pune on land; the navy was founded once the kingdom reached the west coast, to secure access to the resources of the coastal regions.

Part (b): forts secured a land base; the navy secured coastal resources

questions.q: Write a short situation, set in the 17th-century Deccan, that shows a jagir working exactly as the chapter defines it. Your situation must make clear who gives the land, to whom and why, and what the holder does with its income.
questions.a: Sample: 'A sultan of the Deccan gives a village and its fields to Kondaji, a cavalry officer, as a reward for years of loyal service. Kondaji collects taxes from the farmers there. He uses part of the money to look after his family and keeps horsemen ready, so that when the sultan calls for help in a campaign he can send them.' This fits the definition: land given by a ruler to a noble or soldier as a reward for service, with the right to collect taxes for his own needs and to help the ruler.
s: A ruler gives land to a noble or soldier
The reason is reward for service
The holder collects taxes and uses them for his needs and to help the ruler

questions.q: A farmer living near Pune in the 1630s complains to his family about constant hardship. According to the chapter, what was the main cause of hardship for common people in that region at the time?
questions.a: Constant infighting between the Deccan sultans the Marathas served
o: Constant infighting between the Deccan sultans the Marathas served
The Khilji Sultanate's armies overcoming the Yadava capital at Devagiri
Shaista Khan's Mughal army invading the region for three years
Afzal Khan's men raiding villages from hiding places in the mountains

questions.q: Trace five links in how a boy growing up in a jagir at Pune came to rule a kingdom that reached the sea. For each link, say what it added and why the next link depended on it.
questions.a: 1. Upbringing: born in 1630, he grew up at Pune under Jijabai and trusted officials, with values and a good education; this gave him the character and base from which to act. 2. First campaigns (1646): at 16 he captured neglected and unoccupied forts and strengthened them; this gave him a hold over Pune without which no kingdom could grow. 3. A widening aim: his vision of Swarajya grew to political, economic and cultural aspects; this turned a hold on forts into a plan for a sovereign kingdom. 4. The coast and the navy (1657): the kingdom reached the west coast and a navy was founded to secure coastal resources, which Bijapur's merchant ships and the Mughals' limited navy did not match. 5. Defence against bigger armies: with guerrilla warfare he defeated Afzal Khan and routed his army at Pratapgad, which kept the kingdom he had built.
s: Upbringing and what it gave
First forts and why the hold on Pune mattered
The growing vision of Swarajya
The coast and the navy
Guerrilla warfare at Pratapgad protecting what was built

questions.q: Compare a jagir with Swarajya. Define each as the chapter does, then analyse why a young man holding a jagir who sets out to build Swarajya is making a very large change in his position.
questions.a: A jagir was a piece of land given by a king or ruler to someone, usually a noble or soldier, as a reward for service; its holder could collect taxes from the land and use the money to take care of his needs or help the king when needed. Swarajya was a vision of a sovereign kingdom, which grew to cover political, economic and cultural aspects. The holder of a jagir depends on a ruler who gave the land and owes him help; a sovereign kingdom has no such ruler above it. So moving from the Pune jagir, held under the Deccan sultans whom the Marathas served, to Swarajya meant changing from a servant of others to a sovereign, and from land held for a reward to a state covering every part of life.
s: Jagir defined: land given by a ruler as a reward for service
What the jagir holder does: collects taxes and helps the ruler
Swarajya defined: a sovereign kingdom
Swarajya's reach: political, economic and cultural aspects
Analysis: from depending on a ruler to being sovereign, using the Pune jagir under the sultans

questions.a: Coronation: in 1674 he was crowned with full Vedic rites at Raigad, took the title Shri Raja Shiva Chhatrapati and began the Rajyabhisheka shaka era; it gave the Marathas a formal, sovereign kingdom, the formal beginning of the Maratha Empire. Analysis: after his death Aurangzeb executed Sambhaji and captured Raigad itself, so the capital of the crowned kingdom was lost; the kingdom survived because Rajaram could move to Gingee in the south. The coronation gave the Marathas a sovereign state worth defending, and the southern conquest gave that state somewhere to retreat to.
s: Coronation: Vedic rites, title and own era
What it gave: formal sovereignty, the start of the Maratha Empire
Dakshina-digvijaya: northern Tamil Nadu and parts of Karnataka
What it gave: strategic depth against the Mughals
Analysis: Raigad fell after his death but the fight moved to Gingee; one gave a state, the other a place to retreat

questions.q: Analyse Maratha history from Chhatrapati Shivaji's death in 1680 to 1818 in three phases. For each phase, name it, give its key events and the turning point that ended it.
questions.a: Phase 1, survival (1680 to the death of Aurangzeb): Sambhaji became Chhatrapati and was executed by Aurangzeb, who captured Raigad; Rajaram moved to Gingee and the war spread south; the Marathas defended their forts, and Aurangzeb died in the Deccan without subduing them (timeline 1682-1707). Turning point: no longer on the defensive, the Marathas under Tarabai invaded Mughal territories. Phase 2, expansion: the state decentralised, the Peshwa gained great influence, and Bajirao I and Nanasaheb Peshwa led the pan-Indian expansion to Lahore, Attock and Peshawar; despite the disaster at Panipat in 1761 they recovered under Madhavrao I, and Mahadji Shinde retook Delhi in 1771. Phase 3, contest with the British: the Marathas became the chief rivals of the British; the chapter dates three wars from 1775 to 1818, and internal disunity and superior British organisation and technology ended their power in 1818.
s: Phase 1 events: Sambhaji executed, Raigad lost, Gingee, forts held
Turning point 1: Aurangzeb dies without subduing them; Tarabai goes on the offensive
Phase 2 events: decentralisation, Peshwas, expansion to the northwest
Panipat 1761 and recovery, with Delhi retaken in 1771
Phase 3: rivalry with the British, three wars from 1775 to 1818, power ended through disunity and British superiority
